title: Meghan did not let her father see her children to protect them
description: Before today's allegations and the statement from the Duchess of Sussex there was not much at all between Meghan and her father.Quite when the duchess
body: Before today's allegations and the statement from the Duchess of Sussex there was not much at all between Meghan and her father.Quite when the duchess last saw her father Thomas isn't clear. By the time her engagement was announced in 2017, a once-close relationship had cooled.He had moved to Mexico following his retirement in the US and then, as he spoke freely to the media before and after her 2018 wedding, the relationship went into the deep freeze.He said she barely called as he underwent heart surgery, the duchess's people briefed that she had. Then they went silent as he complained in interview after interview that he no longer saw his daughter, had never met Harry nor, later, his grandchildren.Now Meghan has told us why.Thomas Markle gave the first, very large, hint that things would be different within weeks of the announcement of Meghan and Harry's wedding.Instead of accepting the embrace of the Palace - and the media silence that involves - he happily went rogue, giving comments, sometimes commentary, to various media outlets. He had what appeared to be a paid photoshoot whilst claiming that he was being harassed by the media, withdrawing from the wedding just days beforehand as he underwent heart surgery.There was no lack of drama.The interviews and comments never really stopped. Markle was a regular on some broadcast outlets, often complaining that he had no contact with his daughter and son-in-law or, later, his grandchildren.From Meghan came neither comment nor guidance as to why she had cut contact with the father with whom she had once been so close.And into that vacuum rushed theory and supposition - that Meghan was embarrassed by her father, that she and Harry felt their privacy had been compromised by him and so would no longer give him material to recycle, that the old man who was so close to the popular news outlets that tormented them was no longer part of the life they wanted to lead.Those theories became part of the case against Meghan;  that she would sacrifice anyone and anything - even her father - to protect her position and save herself from any embarrassment.That must have stung. Because today, without exactly using the word, she claimed vindication."I hope it can now be understood" she wrote. "That, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them."Meghan says she was informed of the allegations back in 2018. It is understood that it was after her marriage to Harry in May that year. Since then there has only been very limited contact between Meghan and her father - she wrote to him after he underwent surgery in the Philippines late last year.How much all of this changes the perception of Meghan is difficult to tell. Many people have made their minds up about Meghan and the saga with her father is only part of the tangled story of the duchess and the rest of the royal family.But her supporters will see vindication in the allegations - which have been denied by Thomas Markle - and the response that Meghan says she made when she first learned of them.

schema.headline: Meghan did not let her father see her children to protect them

title: Father who killed Oregon school shooter describes anguish over children he couldn't save
description: A father who shot dead a gunman at his two daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described "hearing children pleading for their lives" and h
body: A father who shot dead a gunman at his two daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described "hearing children pleading for their lives" and his anguish over those he could not save.Three students and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student at Silver Rail Elementary School earlier this month. The attacker was then killed by parent Kaylub Giamanco. "I want to apologise for not saving their babies," Giamanco, who has been hailed as a hero, said of his thoughts for the parents of the children killed in an interview with  Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) that aired on Friday. "The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save."Giamanco, 36, said he wanted to meet the victims' families and "cry with them and hold them".He credited a teacher who fought the attacker with giving him the chance to intervene without losing his own life."I would love to give her a hug because that's a real true hero," he said.The students who were killed were all boys, aged five, eight and 11. They were among six people in total who were shot in a classroom at the school, police said. Alongside the teacher who was also killed, another child and a teacher were wounded.Giamanco told OPB the day of the attack began with breakfast and packed lunches. He and his wife spent extra time getting their daughters ready because it was school picture day.The carpenter had taken lunch to work but decided to go home to eat with his wife instead. That decision brought him past the school as the attack began.He initially wondered whether someone carrying a long gun was playing a prank. Then he saw him fire at a pickup truck and head towards the school.Giamanco retrieved a handgun from his vehicle and called emergency services."I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,'" he told the broadcaster.He followed the attacker, who shot through the school's locked glass doors. Hearing children pleading for their lives and more gunfire, Giamanco crawled towards the building."I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do," he said.Giamanco crawled through a shattered window and reached the classroom, where a teacher was struggling with the gunman. He opened the door and fired.Giamanco told OPB he fired again when the attacker reached for his weapon. He then placed his own gun on the ground and raised his hands as an officer appeared.He described feeling like the "last line of defence" between the children and the gunman and said he "was supposed to be there" that day.Afterwards, he called his wife to say he would not be home for lunch and that she needed to get to the school immediately. He then called his mother to tell her what had happened."Mum, I just had to take the life of what I think is might be a child because he ran into my daughter's school with a gun," he said.Police identified the gunman as Griffin J John II - a former pupil who had attended special education classes at the school. His motive remains under investigation.Police said the teacher who confronted the attacker had thrown her phone at him, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said she "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".The youngest victim was Rhoam Summer, 5. His father said the family was "broken and lost".Megan Lambert, 25, the teacher who was killed, was working in what her family described as her "dream job"."She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said. The other two boys have not been publicly named at their families' request.The injured teacher has been named as Becky Drury, 54. She said in a statement shared with US media that the gunman shot her as she tried to shut her classroom door.

schema.headline: Father who killed Oregon school shooter describes anguish over children he couldn't save

title: Macron says deadly shooting near Paris is a 'racist terrorist attack'
description: French President Emmanuel Macron has labelled a gun attack in a Parisian suburb which killed one person and injured five others "a racist terrorist at
body: French President Emmanuel Macron has labelled a gun attack in a Parisian suburb which killed one person and injured five others "a racist terrorist attack".Macron said the attack was a "turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation" - the first time there has ever been a random racial killing like this.The attack unfolded over some 15 minutes with the attacker opening fire from his car - first in Trappes to the south-west of Paris, and then in nearby La Verrière - appearing to target people of migrant origin. He was subsequently arrested.Three of those injured, including a 12-year-old girl, remain in a serious condition.Visiting the scene of the attack in Trappes, Macron said people had been targeted for their skin colour or religion and urged the public not to give an inch in the face of what he called "ideologies taking root".The exact motive remains unclear, but the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said the incident appeared to be "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise".The suspect has been named in French media as Kevin T who, according to PNAT, had four previous convictions which had been "automatically expunged".The 39-year-old was known to police but not to France's intelligence services, local media report.He was not on a list of individuals considered to be a serious threat to French security, the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office told BFMTV.A member of the suspect's "immediate family circle" was also taken into custody on Friday, it added.The Mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, said that "an individual fired shots from his vehicle at several people he encountered" on Friday morning.The gunman drove through several neighbourhoods in a grey Renault Clio, according to witnesses. Rabeh said he had  "fired randomly" with the seeming intent of causing "as many casualties as possible... he wanted to cause carnage", he said.The mayor said people had been targeted at a petrol station, a medical centre and a playground in Trappes before the attacker had driven on to nearby La Verrière.A police union official said the suspect had been detained in La Verrière on the main N10 road that runs through the town.

schema.headline: Macron says deadly shooting near Paris is a 'racist terrorist attack'

title: Jordan church shooting leaves seven dead, officials say
description: Seven people have been killed in an attack on a funeral in central Jordan, officials have said.At least 34 others were injured as gunmen opened fire o
body: Seven people have been killed in an attack on a funeral in central Jordan, officials have said.At least 34 others were injured as gunmen opened fire on a church in Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday.The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing. No-one has admitted carrying out the attack.In a news conference, Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said authorities were working to apprehend the perpetrators which he described as a "group of extremists".Jordan's King Abdullah II said authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties".Initial reports indicated seven people had been killed in the attack. A government spokesperson later said six people had died, before officials again revised the death toll to seven.CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church.Two of the attackers are seen making their way on to what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns.Separate footage believed to be from the aftermath of the attack appears to show several dead and wounded bodies on the ground amid chaotic scenes.Witnesses have described scenes of panic inside the church as people threw themselves under pews searching for cover, moving away from the windows.Prayers and screams could be heard throughout the building as some tried to flee.Khalid al-Mdanat was at the church and told BBC Arabic the attack lasted around 15 minutes with "people trying to flee while the shooting was still active"."People began pushing and throwing themselves to the ground," he said."Some were taking cover, some were cradling the dead, others were holding their sons close, some were grabbing their children and fleeing, while others were holding onto their friends who were with them at the church."He said the gunmen left through the church doors and fled in a pickup truck "firing as they went".Another witness said: "I heard something as if a war had just started."I thought it was an electrical short circuit. I looked, people lying on the ground, wounded. The scene was catastrophic."A woman in the church said explosions rang out seconds after a prayer."The sound of machine guns started, and the sound of glass. We began to realise that something was happening."People started screaming. The witness described how the situation "continued to escalate for 10 continuous minutes". Once she ran out the church she said "bodies were all in the courtyards".Al-Faraya has described the incident as "painful and horrific" and "unparalleled in the history of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan".There was a heavy security presence at the entrance to a hospital treating people injured in the incident in Karak, amid an atmosphere charged with anger among residents of the governorate, particularly the families of those injured and killed.Many looked distressed as roads were closed around the facility and people were forced to park their cars and continue on foot.Security measures were also tightened ahead of the visit by King Abdullah II to check on the injured.The atmosphere around the hospital remained tense as the sound of crying and shouting was heard as families mourned their loved ones.Many people appear shocked, frightened and angry. Some expressed frustration at what they described as "a failure to take a tougher approach towards terrorists".Karak has a sizeable Christian community in the majority-Muslim Jordan.Such violence is rare in the country, but deadly attacks have been carried out in the past.Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun, a Christian head of state, said the "heinous terrorist attack" on the church "violated the sanctity of death and funeral mourners, contradicts all religious and humanitarian values," according to Lebanese media.Additional reporting by Majdi Gousous, BBC Arabic.

schema.headline: Jordan church shooting leaves seven dead, officials say

title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
description: The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.As part of Wedn
body: The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats."AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said."I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI."One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops."That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said."By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing £200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.The Chancellor's plans to boost AI spending will also see an additional £120m committed to the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI).Established by the former Conservative government in 2023, the lab evaluates the risks of the most advanced and powerful models - and has been championed for its role in helping build a collaborative and open approach to AI testing.The additional funding announced by the Chancellor will aim to help ensure the lab can continue its efforts and work, particularly amid growing calls for technical standards and guardrails for AI development.It will come alongside a £60m investment in what it coined a "National Cyber Shield" which it said would use agentic AI to boost cyber-defences, and £70m funding towards a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.This, it said, would harness AI tools to detect cyber vulnerabilities across the UK's critical infrastructure and economy.It comes after the UK government revealed it was among organisations around the world to have taken some sites offline as a precaution after critical flaws were surfaced in a popular programming language.Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side scripting language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks.There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far.But experts have warned that the incident shows how quickly and easily bugs which have lain long dormant may be surfaced - and potentially exploited - using AI.

schema.headline: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab

title: Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water
description: The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.With storms battering the U
body: The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.With storms battering the UK, and in the wake of online disruption caused by a major security flaw, Andy Burnham said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common".The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.Burnham added: "It's not about panicking... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."At Labour's conference last month, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner joked that her emergency box, external would include a bottle of wine.She said she'd include: "Mascara, concealer, I don't know, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, a tin of baked beans because you've gotta have some baked beans, and I like a good tin of custard as well so I think that'll keep me going for a while."Asked whether he agreed with her, Burnham told BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley: "Well, I'm not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you're in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you've done the hard work. "But I'll stick to the basics I think - I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup. "I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets, I'm not sure I can get by for too long without those."Last month, the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis and said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.The chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, also told the BBC the UK is being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, Burnham denied the government had failed to properly prepare, saying: "No, we're having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we're living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common."Obviously, weather events, and we're in a situation today where the UK is facing storms and obviously, we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now."It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments. So we are having that conversation about resilience."A checklist drawn up by the government recommends having nine litres of water per person – enough for three days – along with non-perishable food such as tinned meat and vegetables or dried fruit.The government suggests having an FM radio, either battery or wind-up. During a national crisis, the BBC would prioritise broadcasting news, as well as health and safety information. In the event of a severe power cut, FM radio will be the best way to receive these updates.The list also suggests hand sanitiser, wet wipes and toiletries, food for any pets, supplies for any babies, a torch, blankets, a charged power bank for devices, cash in case payment systems collapse, a first aid kit and copies of important documents.Earlier, Treasury minister James Murray told BBC Breakfast he has not yet followed the government's guidance on stockpiling supplies to prepare for a crisis.He said he had a stockpile of coffee, but pointed out that neighbouring countries including Ireland, France and the Netherlands had given the same guidance "for quite a long time".He added: "I'm not going to pretend I've followed all that advice myself yet."Speaking on the same programme, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she was "stocked up for the week at any time".She said the previous Conservative government had issued similar advice on preparing for emergencies, but added: "What I'm more concerned about is that it doesn't look like [the government] are explaining what the risks we are under are, and what they are doing about the big things. "Families can stock up but what's going on with defence, the cyber attacks, the hybrid warfare? The money to look after the country has not been forthcoming."

schema.headline: Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water

title: White House says Melania Trump brokers truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
description: Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this yearByJaroslav Lukiv and Bernd Debusmann J
body: Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this yearByJaroslav Lukiv and Bernd Debusmann JrWhite House reporterUS First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said.It said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" without medicine, food and clean water would begin on 29 October.Ukraine and Russia confirmed the deal was agreed to evacuate residents and deliver aid. They both said their forces would stop firing at 02:00 GMT on 27 October.Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Trapped between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east, residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive.Figure caption, Trump: First lady's 'initiative' led to truce for Ukraine cityThe White House statement said Melania Trump and one of her representatives had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire"."Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying."Residents who wish to evacuate will receive co-ordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible".The statement did not say how long the ceasefire would be in place for.Davyd Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads President Volodymyr Zelensky's party in parliament, later said "an operation to unblock the settlement of Oleshky and its surroundings will begin in the near future"."To achieve this goal, a ceasefire will be achieved in the near future, as announced by the First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump," he said.In Russia, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman confirmed that, "those who wish to do so will be able to leave this settlement".Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutionsLast month, some of the remaining Oleshky residents told the BBC harrowing accounts of how they were surviving in the city that was being constantly shelled and cut off from food and water.They said that children remaining in wider Oleshky were suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services and were "degrading" without access to education.Many also told the BBC there was only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.The local population was living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.Ukraine says it has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.The Kremlin in September acknowledged that Oleshky was facing "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now  Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.It is also one of a number of settlements where thousands of people lost their homes to a massive flooding caused by the collapse of Nova Khakovka Dam in 2023. Ukraine and its allies accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Melania Trump worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to agree the ceasefire, the White House said.While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.In August 2025, Melania Trump penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".Although she did not mention Ukraine by name, just days later at the White House Zelensky handed over a letter from his wife Olena, thanking her for her efforts on children.In a rare public appearance in October the same year, the US first lady said that Putin had answered directly in writing and that her representatives were working with the Russian president's team to repatriate Ukrainian children from Russia and vice versa.Some 34 children have reportedly been returned since 2025, including five this July.According to US President Donald Trump, his wife has also privately expressed scepticism about Putin and his desire to achieve peace."I'd get home, I'd say, 'First lady, I had the most wonderful talk with Vladimir. I think we're finished'," Trump said in July last year."And then I'll turn on the television, or she'll say to me one time, 'Wow, that's strange because they just bombed a nursing home.'"Additional reporting by Olga Malchevska

schema.headline: White House says Melania Trump brokers truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'

title: Ruins of city hall a symbol of France divided by protests
description: For weeks, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young, have engaged in protests that have only increased in size and scope. What started off as a d
body: For weeks, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young, have engaged in protests that have only increased in size and scope. What started off as a demonstration over the poor state of high schools has expanded to a general frustration, even anger, over how challenging and expensive life has become.In the backdrop is a daunting fiscal deficit, one of the biggest in Europe, and political candidates from across the spectrum claiming to have the answers ahead of presidential elections in six months' time.In the middle is a centrist government, which is short on solutions, a majority in the National Assembly and time. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu visited Limoges on Friday evening.Officials have banned demonstrations in various cities and promised to boost police numbers over the weekend to avoid a repeat of the rioting. That includes in Limoges, where overnight curfews have been announced, along with a limit on gatherings to 10 people in the centre.Proud as the French are of their politics being rooted in street demonstrations, many in Limoges felt the town hall's destruction went far beyond the parameters of reasonable protest. But not everyone.Whether the destruction of Limoges town hall changes the course and tone of an increasingly polarised political debate depends on who you ask."Of course it was really sad, it's a symbol of the republic, but what is more important: a town hall or people living in poverty?" asks Alexander, 24.It is student night at the Lord John pub, and Alexander is one of several wearing a faluche, a colourful, traditional French student beret. Many chatting under the mist from their vapes took part in the demonstrations last weekend.I ask Alexander whether the widespread looting and fires seen last weekend, with €500,000 (£420,000) of reported damage in Limoges, helped his argument?"For some people it's a catastrophe and some things are not acceptable," he admits.Jade, a 19-year-old, medical student, has a similar opinion: "I think burning the town hall is sad, but it's not the saddest part of the protests."She complains of having to live on €300 per month. "I feel we are not respected as young adults."Their views on the town hall's fate are not replicated in Limoges' imposing market halls, where neat, narrow timbers sitting upon studded steel girders have been painted a duck-egg blue, using the same engineering approach as the Eiffel Tower.This has been a "week of chaos" that 63-year-old Jean Roger Faucher would like to forget.In a region renowned for producing beef, his family has run his fishmonger stool here for more than a century."It left us stunned," he says. "I got married in the town hall, so it had an unimaginable effect on us."Asked whether he had sympathy for the protesters, Faucher said it was more complicated than that."On one side you have people with grievances you can understand, but from the moment there is vandalism and the lives of local residents are put at risk, then we can't accept it," he adds.Among those tending to their iced displays of fresh produce or quietly sipping a steaming coffee, there is a desire for the temperature of the demonstrations to decrease."Of course, life is expensive!' says Pascale Vuylsteke, 59. "Life isn't all a calm river, it's complicated, but we grit our teeth and we work," she tells me leaning over shelves of butchered pork.Pascale says she works 100 hours a week and struggles to understand why so many others have taken to the streets so easily.Limoges has found itself at the heart of social action before. In the 19th Century, around the time the town hall was built, the development of its industries, notably in porcelain, led to it becoming a major centre for the French labour movement.In 2026, the town sits centre-stage once more in a political rupture, although there is a broad hope that the loss of a prominent piece of its history will steer the demonstrations away from destruction and back to debate.With France's political polarisation set to continue and further protests planned, it is a scenario far from assured.Additional reporting by Paul Pradier.

schema.headline: Ruins of city hall a symbol of France divided by protests

title: Are California voters about to impose world's first tax on billionaires?
description: Image source, ReutersBySareen HabeshianReporting fromLos AngelesFew places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US stat
body: Image source, ReutersBySareen HabeshianReporting fromLos AngelesFew places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for glamour, coastal mega-mansions and being home to many rich and famous.Now voters are about to decide if the mega-rich among them - names that include media mogul Oprah Winfrey, Meta head Mark Zuckerberg, Skims cofounder and reality television star Kim Kardashian and filmmaker George Lucas - should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.Proposition 40 is aimed at levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of all of California's billionaires.There are a little more than 200 such individuals in the state - but that hasn't stopped the measure from dividing leaders and causing some of its ultra-wealthy residents to flee. One billionaire businessman says he's brought jobs to California, but the proposition made him feel "a little bit like I wasn't wanted".But the vote is also offering regular everyday residents a voice on an issue that has riled politics for decades."I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap.The state has the largest economy in the country - and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the whole of the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the globe. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps.Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system.Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill."If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she told the BBC.Image source, Getty ImagesWhile the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor.Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax, the Los Angeles Times reports, external.California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.A September poll, external from the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents.California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year.While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries – Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs.Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue, she said.In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the country in 2022, external than in the preceding 13 years combined. A study on Switzerland, external found that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly  given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth taxThe California measure, if approved, would apply retroactively to those with a net worth of at least $1bn who resided in California as of 1 January 2026. At least six of the state's 200 plus billionaires have reportedly left California ahead of that deadline to avoid the tax.They include Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, venture capitalist Peter Thiel, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Hankey Group founder Don Hankey.Hankey, a Los Angeles billionaire who has lived in California all his life, told Forbes he left for the state of Nevada as a result of the proposed wealth tax."I think we've created a lot of jobs in California. We have a few thousand people working for us and we have a profit sharing plan. And I have to leave the state," he added, saying the measure made him feel like he wasn't "wanted" in the state.Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg told the company's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California over the proposed tax. To prevent him from leaving the state - where the company is headquartered - Meta agreed to a new stock deal that gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn, even more shares in the company to make up for the billions he would lose if the measure passes in November. Estimates say he could owe as much as $12.5bn.DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, who has an estimated net worth of $1.6bn, has called the measure "stupid" and wrote on X that "proposals like this make it irresponsible for me not to plan leaving the state".Meanwhile, businessman Tom Steyer, who ran an unsuccessful bid for California governor earlier this year, is one of the few billionaires who has said, external he would vote in favour of the tax. Steyer said that although he believes the way the measure is written is "problematic", it is necessary to protect vulnerable Californians.Huang, too, has expressed support of paying the levy."I don't mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I'm okay with that," the Nvidia chief executive said in an interview with the BBC's news partner in the US, CBS. "I am the ultimate American Dream."Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a vocal champion against income inequality, has campaigned in support of Prop 40.While at a Los Angeles rally, Sanders said billionaires "believe, like the monarchs of the 19th century, that they have a God-given right to rule". "They have all the wealth; they got all the power, and who the hell do you think you are challenging them? Well, I think on Nov 3 they're going to learn a very powerful lesson".Income inequality in the US is at some of its highest levels, external in over three decades, with the top 1% of households owning nearly 32% of all US wealth in the third quarter of 2025. It is also near historic highs in California.Economic inequality is a concern among most Californians, with 72% believing that the gap between the rich and poor is widening and a similar share holding that state government should do more to reduce the gap, according to a statewide survey, external from the Public Policy Institute of California.Trebbi says it is an "anti-elite, anti-system sentiment that is behind a policy" like Prop 40."This is really not about Prop 40," he says. It's about trying to "re-balance the scale a little bit".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, US Senator Bernie Sanders speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on 5 October in Los Angeles.

schema.headline: Are California voters about to impose world's first tax on billionaires?

title: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesByJack Grey and Freya Scott-TurnerDo you have three days' worth of food and water in your home?That is what the gove
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesByJack Grey and Freya Scott-TurnerDo you have three days' worth of food and water in your home?That is what the government has told all of us to have on hand to get through a national emergency, as well as some other basic items.Its "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need to get through a rocky few days.On Friday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unexpected events "seem to becoming more common" and everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".As one expert warns the UK is "light years" behind our neighbours when it comes to preparing for major disruption, we've drilled down into what you need and why.What is on the 'Be Ready' checklist?The government recommends having enough supplies in the kitchen to last three days, including bottled water and non-perishable foods.Wet wipes, a torch and cash are also recommended - you can scroll through below to see the full list.Disaster planning expert Professor Lucy Easthope said the goal of asking household to prepare is to make it easier for emergency service to cope in the event of a national emergency.For example, the government says people who need medication should have an extra supply just in case. Prof Easthope says: "If people have got their heart pills for an extra 48 hours, it stops [response crews] from having to immediately find an emergency pharmacist."While the latest government campaign only launched on Thursday, some people are well ahead of the game.Speaking to Radio 5 Live, Bridgette Clamp, who lives in near Penzance in Cornwall, said she has stocked up on "lots of tinned goods" as well as "flour, yeast and everything to bake bread". "We're rocking and rolling," she says.Image source, Bridgette ClampImage caption, Bridgette says she also bought generators and water pumps following Storm Goretti earlier this year One woman, who spoke to 5 Live anonymously, said she bought "loads and loads" of emergency food - but ended up eating it before it was strictly necessary. Like others, she wondered if the government was "scaremongering", adding: "I don't know but I've certainly bought into it."Rob, who lives off-grid in north Wales, told the programme he has stocked up on so many supplies he "wouldn't even notice" if a disaster struck.But he said he still felt there was "a bit of scaremongering" going on and wondered if he would ever need it all.Why is the government telling people to stockpile now?Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the advice - which is similar to guidance issued by the previous government - was not triggered by any "particular piece of intelligence", but rather about improving "national resilience" more generally.The government's announcement focused on extreme weather events, which are becoming more frequent because of man-made climate change - but Streeting also referred to the threat of "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, and supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".Prof Easthope said she has been lobbying the government to launch this sort of campaign for "about 16 years".She said successive governments have been hesitant of "putting out information that might cause tension" - and speculated that this advice may have been "rushed" out ahead of Storm Austen hitting the UK.Image source, Lucy EastmanImage caption, Expert Prof Lucy Easthope says the UK is playing "massive catch up" to other nations in disaster preparedness While many of us will already have a stash of tinned food in the cupboards, fewer homes are likely to have a store of bottled water.Paul from Torquay, Devon, said to Radio 5 Live: "Who on earth carries three day supply of water?"He added: "I think they've made it our responsibility, rather than their responsibility."Do other countries have similar emergency advice?Prof Easthope described the UK as "light years" behind neighbouring countries when it comes to preparedness. "Countries like Scandinavia, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, they've been good at this for years," she said.France advises people to store 72-hours' worth of food, while the German government says homes should have enough supplies to last for a 10-day period. "This is one area where I'm very comfortable saying we are playing massive catch-up," added Easthope.Awareness campaigns such as "think 72 hours" make a big difference in the US, Australia and "all around Europe", she said.However, in the UK, she said disaster messaging often gets parodied, or governments are accused of "panic-mongering". "We have seen the pendulum shift" in recent years, she adds, saying that "we are now seeing people recognise this" as an issue that needs tackling.

schema.headline: Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

title: UK state pension: How does it compare with other countries?
description: Image source, 10000 hours Getty ImagesByDharshini DavidDeputy economics editorGetting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fun
body: Image source, 10000 hours Getty ImagesByDharshini DavidDeputy economics editorGetting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged. With that cost set to balloon further, the debate over whether that is sustainable, or fair, has raged for a while.Andy Burnham intends to start a new system in a few years, which would see the state pension increase by at least inflation or 2.5%, and remove the automatic annual link with average earnings. It will likely mean less generous increases, although it will keep track with earnings growth over the longer term.But are pensioners being short-changed in other ways? How do we compare with other countries? One way of measuring that is to look at how generous the typical pension is relative to workers' average earnings - the replacement rate. The OECD considers the outlook for those born at the start of the millennium in different countries on average wages, and assumes the pension system as it existed in 2022 is in place.On that basis, looking at the basic state pension, retirement benefits in the UK look low compared with other wealthy countries. And that is even when you consider that our system compels workers to be automatically enrolled in occupational schemes. If you consider both of those, then after tax, UK retirement benefits would be 54.2% of average UK earnings, compared with an average of 63.2% across wealthy countries.But then there is income from other occupational and personal pensions, which are more prevalent in the UK. Include those and the gap narrows. However, that does also mean that those relying on just the state pension for their incomes are a fair bit worse off than many retired people elsewhere.So does that make the case for boosting spending on public pensions in the UK? Well, the amount spent on the state pension is set to top £150bn a year, the single most expensive benefit to fund. But other figures from the OECD show that the UK state spends a lower amount on total retirement benefits, relative to the size of its economy, than the average wealthy country.But there are two issues to consider. Firstly, this is about political choices, and the UK chooses to dedicate larger amounts to items such as universal healthcare.And secondly, with ageing populations, the OECD reckons the amount needed for pensions may be set to soar in many nations by 2060 (the exceptions largely being those that are deploying changes). Its predictions for the UK are likely to rise by less under the revised triple lock system being put in place by Andy Burnham but it may still mean more borrowing. As it is, £1 in every £13 the UK government spends is to pay the interest on existing debt. And countries with more generous pensions, such as Italy, have faced pressure to reform.So in many ways, with auto-enrolment into workplace pensions, the UK appears to be ahead of the game in insisting on universal privately funded pensions for workers. But that system raises another issue: the gender pension gap. The gender pension gap is the difference between the average pension income of men and women aged 65 and over, as a percentage of men's average pension income.It found that the typical gap in most wealthy countries is around 22.8% in favour of men. But in the UK women typically get a pension that is a third less than what a man gets - in the main, due to the reliance on private pensions - although it should be noted that the most recent data the OECD has for the UK is for 2021.Women are more likely to have received lower pay over the course of their working lives, taken career breaks or worked part time. And the hit to pension pots can be stark.So step back and look at the big picture and British pensioners - and those who have yet to retire - may feel others have it better elsewhere. But the message from all of this isn't to dwell on outrage but to take action. The state pension has become more generous over the years, but if you want to enjoy the same kind of retirement as those elsewhere, get saving.That is - if you can, and if you haven't left it too late.

schema.headline: UK state pension: How does it compare with other countries?

title: Woman at centre of Cornell University rape inquiry in 'constant fear', lawyer says
description: The life of a woman who filed a lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped at a Cornell University fraternity house has been completely upended, her l
body: The life of a woman who filed a lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped at a Cornell University fraternity house has been completely upended, her lawyer has said. Speaking to the BBC ahead of a hearing in the civil case on Friday in New York, her lawyer Thomas Giuffra said: "She feels under fire."The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former school and the fraternity over the alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.When the case went viral, a series of "I am Jane Doe" solidarity posts appeared, but  there was a separate campaign aimed at unmasking her and defending the men, who have all denied any wrongdoing. The men, who are also being sued by the woman, have not been charged with any crimes. With initial proceedings now under way in the civil case, Giuffra told the BBC that these last few weeks have been "a very hard time" for his client, who isn't doing a lot beyond "surviving".Her decision to sue was rooted in a desire for closure and to take power back, he said.Giufrra visited Jane Doe this week and found that she hadn't been sleeping well – relying on medication to get rest.Now in trauma therapy, he says she doesn't feel safe in her own home following malicious threats that were directed at her and her family.After her address was published online without her consent, someone called in a fake emergency that led to police in full tactical gear drawing assault rifles on her father, her friend and her brother at their family home."It's just constant fear," he said. He added that despite this her resolve hadn't been shaken and she remains determined to overhaul the university system at Cornell, and across the country, to protect survivors.Cornell University, after initially defending its disciplinary measures, acknowledged it fell short in its handling of Jane Doe's case.After facing intense pressure, the college's president announced that fraternity parties would be suspended until the end of the academic year to allow for a thorough review to determine whether and how they can safely continue. The school also said it would add sexual assault investigators to its police force.Giuffra, however, says he is surprised that Cornell has not reached out to him and believes they have been focused solely on "damage control". He says any agreement with Cornell to resolve the civil lawsuit will need to include "steps to ensure there are no more Jane Does" and if there are, that they are going to be supported.The BBC contacted Cornell for comment who directed us to the university's previous statements and comments on its internal investigation in 2024.New York's governor Kathy Hochul appointed a special prosecutor, New York's Attorney General Letitia James, to oversee a reopened investigation into whether criminal charges are warranted.Giuffra expects it will take a long time to do a proper investigation but is concerned that they will be going after evidence that is now "stale"."A lot of the communication was on Snapchat, Snapchat goes away," he told the BBC. "The best time to get evidence is around the time of the crime and that just didn't happen."However, Giuffra believes he can win the civil case against the university, the men and others, where the burden of proof is lower than a criminal case. Civil cases require a preponderance of the evidence, that it's more likely than not it happened, while criminal cases require proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Recent high profile cases have shown the way juries evaluate consent can be unpredictable."I wouldn't have taken the case if I didn't think it was a strong case that I could win and get her some closure."

schema.headline: Woman at centre of Cornell University rape inquiry in 'constant fear', lawyer says

title: Israeli forces begin demolishing Palestinian buildings in Hebron after two Israeli soldiers shot dead
description: The incident has already begun to influence the ongoing election campaign, with Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - sa
body: The incident has already begun to influence the ongoing election campaign, with Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - saying that his Likud party would cancel campaign events which had been set for Friday morning. Speaking later from the scene, Netanyahu said that the military would "demolish this place and completely transform it," referring to the Hebron neighbourhood where the attackers are said to have come from. It is common for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment. Netanyahu likened his plans to previous operations in West Bank refugee camps where residential buildings were demolished and thousands were displaced. He also said he had reviewed plans for the largest military operation in the West Bank in decades - though did not say when it could be carried out. He added that he had imposed cordons around the city of Hebron - which has around 200,000 residents - and the nearby city of Halhul. Netanyahu's far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for Israel to launch a campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza or Lebanon," while far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir called for Israel to dismantle the Palestinian Authority. On Thursday, Foreign Minister Israel Katz accused opposition leaders of undermining the government by criticising Netanyahu's warnings of an attack ahead of the election, saying they would be "responsible" for any future attack on the country.Opposition chiefs, including frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, offered their condolences to the families of the killed troops and praised those who killed the attackers.The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle, and that they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there. At least 96 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year, according to the UN. Four Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians there over the same period, the UN says - not including those killed in Friday's attack.

schema.headline: Israeli forces begin demolishing Palestinian buildings in Hebron after two Israeli soldiers shot dead

title: Vincent Kompany: Bayern Munich manager taken to hospital after collapsing
description: Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital after collapsing as he watched the club's second team train on Friday.The 40-year-old had
body: Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital after collapsing as he watched the club's second team train on Friday.The 40-year-old had been unwell with a virus and missed the pre-match news conference on Tuesday prior to Bayern's Champions League game against Arsenal.The former Manchester City and Belgium defender was subsequently on the touchline for the match on Wednesday.Reports in Germany say Kompany is in a stable condition in hospital."Vincent Kompany required medical attention after collapsing during an FC Bayern reserve team training session on Friday," said a statement from the Bundesliga club., external "The first-team head coach was watching the second string's session. "Kompany is undergoing thorough examinations in hospital and will remain under medical care. "His coaching staff will oversee training and match activities until further notice."Bayern's next game is against Freiburg in the German top flight on Sunday."Vincent Kompany's health is our top priority. We at FC Bayern will do everything we can to ensure his speedy recovery," said Bayern sporting director Max Eberl."Vinnie is receiving all the necessary medical care and support, and all the time he needs. "His coaching team, in whom we have complete confidence, will take over his duties. All of us at FC Bayern wish Vinnie a speedy recovery."Aaron Danks, one of Kompany's assistants, took the pre-match news conference for Bayern before the Arsenal game.German football journalist Taufig Khalil told BBC Radio 5 Live that Kompany had been "suffering with the virus for about a week".He added: "The thing started last weekend on Saturday against Leipzig, and that's the first time we saw Vincent Kompany [when] he didn't look very well. "He didn't do the press conference after, and Max Eberl told us that he's suffering with a virus."Everybody was really surprised that Vincent Kompany was standing there with his black jacket in the pouring rain of Munich on Wednesday night against Arsenal. Everybody expected Aaron Danks to be there. "The problem was that maybe you couldn't bench Vincent Kompany, the game was too important for him."Bayern Munich just told us that he's in stable conditions. There was a helicopter involved in the whole thing, which landed on the training ground at Bayern Munich, but he was not brought into the hospital by helicopter. They brought him with a medical car and he will be now there."Kompany left his role as Burnley manager to take over at Bayern in May 2024, succeeding current England manager Thomas Tuchel.He had won the Championship with Burnley in 2022-23 and, despite the Clarets being relegated from the Premier League under him the following season, Kompany was appointed by the Bundesliga club.He has led Bayern to the German top-flight title in the past two seasons and reached the 2025-26 Champions League semi-finals before being beaten by eventual winners Paris St-Germain.Kompany spent 11 years at Manchester City as a player, winning four Premier League titles, two FA Cups and four League Cups.  "Everyone at Manchester City is wishing a speedy recovery to our former captain and club legend, Vincent Kompany," said City in a post on social media. "Get well soon, Vinny.""Everyone here at Burnley FC sends our best wishes to Vincent and we wish him a speedy recovery," said a Burnley statement.

schema.headline: Vincent Kompany: Bayern Munich manager taken to hospital after collapsing

title: The Prem: Newcastle Red Bulls 17-3 Sale Sharks - Christian Wade equals Chris Ashton's try record
description: If talks beforehand had centred on Wade's potential march into the record books, it was typical that there were barely any chances for anyone in the f
body: If talks beforehand had centred on Wade's potential march into the record books, it was typical that there were barely any chances for anyone in the first half.Almost half an hour passed without Wade even touching the ball, a period during which England fly-half George Ford kicked a penalty for the visitors for the only points before half-time.It was scrappy and narrow in difficult, gusty conditions which invited a high-kicking game early from both sides - yet there was something for defensive purists to cling to, with both sides withstanding pressure in the shadow of their own posts.Both teams had also turned down the chance for long penalties and after one too many Sale transgressions for using hands on the ground, Newcastle again elected for Brett Connon to kick towards the corner, not the posts, from 40 metres out.It was that decision that finally delivered the platform for Newcastle to first hammer away on the left then eventually go through hands out wide right to where a grateful Wade was waiting.Josh Hodge added the extras to give Newcastle a 7-3 lead and he extended that to 10-3 with a simple close chip over after Sale were again penalised, this time for entering from the side.From there, the next score seemed pivotal and it was much to the home crowd's relief when a rumbling, powerful maul allowed ball-carrier McGuigan to drop down behind the line just after the hour.Hodge's left foot fired a low conversion under the gusting wind to increase the advantage to 17-3 with 12 minutes to go to secure the win - a result that leaves Harlequins as the only team yet to win a match in the Prem this season.Newcastle coach Dan McFarland, speaking to BBC Radio Newcastle:"I am buzzing about the performance. I felt a lot of effort went into that and a lot of physicality in that game as we knew there would be against Sale. It was a battle and that first half was tough."We had a lot of chances down in their 22 but we weren't patient enough and at the end of the half we had to put in a real effort in our own 22 to keep the score at 3-0. We showed our resilience and score a couple of good tries and to fight back, reset and go again was what pleased me the most."There is no turning point here - this is a long journey. Wins are very difficult to come by in this league. But we are not going to get ahead of ourselves. There is a lot in that game we need to grow."It is not relief. It is not euphoria. We are definitely pleased that all the effort and hard work we have put in paid off in getting a victory - but we roll in next week and go again."On Wade equalling the Prem try-scoring record: "He is a high-energy player and high-energy guy. He knows how to find the tryline, which is what all good wingers do."I watched him right at the end of the game when we were in their 22 and he's buzzing because he was thinking that might be the opportunity to get one ahead."He will get there, goodness willing. He is a tremendous guy and he deserves it."Newcastle: Hodge; Wade, Harris, Rigg, Kok; Connon, Benitez Cruz; Rakete-Stones, McGuigan, Millar Mills, Usher, Tuima, Hicks, Christie, Sotutu.Replacements: Togiatama, West, Moreno, Baker, Leatherbarrow, Graham, Elliott, Henry.Sale: Carpenter; Roebuck, Marchant, Maasi-White, O'Flaherty; Ford, Hanson; N Smith, Cowan-Dickie, Francis, Van Rhyn, Bamber, Tshiunza, B Curry, T Curry.Replacements: Jibulu, McIntyre, Opoku-Fordjour, Canakaivata, Dugdale, Lozowski, Louw, Reed.Referee: Matthew Carley.

schema.headline: The Prem: Newcastle Red Bulls 17-3 Sale Sharks - Christian Wade equals Chris Ashton's try record
